internship.title: Web Application Development Internship
internship.description: An engineering-oriented internship in which interns learn and apply the core practices needed to design, build, test, secure, and deploy maintainable server-side web applications. The program moves from HTTP and Java foundations through Spring MVC, persistence, authentication and authorization, API integration, automated testing, debugging, observability, containerization, and an independent capstone. The internship is intentionally organized around realistic work products and reviewable engineering tasks rather than treating the material as a passive course.
prerequisites: Basic programming experience with variables, methods, classes, collections, and exceptions.
Basic HTML and CSS knowledge and familiarity with browser developer tools.
Basic SQL concepts including SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, primary keys, foreign keys, and joins.
Basic command-line usage and Git familiarity.
A local development environment capable of running Java, Maven, and Docker as applicable.
objectives: Build a maintainable Java web application using Spring MVC and clear application-layer boundaries.
Persist relational data with PostgreSQL, JPA, repositories, constraints, migrations, and transaction boundaries.
Implement secure session-based authentication and server-side authorization with Spring Security.
Design and consume a focused JSON API with validation and stable DTO-based responses.
Write unit and MVC/security tests and use reproducible debugging techniques.
Externalize configuration and package the application with Docker Compose.
Document the architecture, setup, troubleshooting approach, security controls, and release workflow.
Complete a substantial independent capstone that integrates the internship competencies.

competencies.evidence: HTTP request/response analysis, forms, status codes, redirects, and browser debugging.

competencies.name: Java/Spring implementation
competencies.evidence: Layered controllers, services, repositories, validation, configuration, and exception handling.

competencies.name: Persistence engineering
competencies.evidence: Relational schema design, JPA entities, repositories, transactions, indexes, and migration practice.

competencies.name: Application security
competencies.evidence: Encoded passwords, session authentication, CSRF protection, role and ownership authorization, safe errors, and secret handling.

competencies.name: Testing and debugging
competencies.evidence: JUnit/Mockito unit tests, MVC/security tests, reproducible failures, root-cause analysis, and regression tests.

competencies.name: Engineering workflow
competencies.evidence: Git branches, focused commits, pull requests, issue-style tasks, documentation, and release checklists.

competencies.name: Operational readiness
competencies.evidence: Environment-driven configuration, health checks, Docker/Compose packaging, logging guidance, and rollback considerations.

modules.title: Engineering Foundations and Web Architecture
modules.description: Build the habits and mental model needed to work on maintainable server-side web applications: HTTP request/response flow, HTML forms, Git workflow, Java/Spring project structure, and clean layering.
objectives: Explain how a browser request moves through a servlet-based application and back to a rendered response.
Use Git branches, focused commits, and pull requests to manage internship work.
Create a Spring Boot project with a clear controller-service-repository boundary.
Model requirements as small, testable work items and document implementation decisions.

lessons.title: HTTP, HTML Forms, and the Server-Side Request Cycle
lessons.description: Trace a browser submission through HTTP, controller binding, validation, business logic, and an HTML response. The intern learns why method, status code, content type, and form semantics matter before touching framework abstractions.
learningObjectives: Explain GET versus POST using the safety/idempotence properties relevant to form submissions.
Read request methods, headers, parameters, cookies, and response status codes during development.
Describe the role of a servlet filter, DispatcherServlet, controller, service, and view renderer in a Spring MVC request.

notes.text: A request is a contract

The browser sends a method, target, headers, and optionally a body. The server returns a status line, headers, and a body. Framework code sits between those wire-level facts and application objects; understanding the wire model makes debugging much easier.

items: Use GET for retrieval and other safe read operations; use POST when a form causes a state change.
A redirect after a successful POST can prevent accidental duplicate form submission when the user refreshes.
Do not trust form values merely because they came from your own page; clients can submit arbitrary values.

practicals.title: Trace a Form Submission
practicals.description: Use browser developer tools and a small Spring MVC endpoint to identify the request method, form body, redirect, and final rendered response.
steps: Create a minimal POST form with a CSRF token rendered by Thymeleaf.
Submit the form and inspect the Network panel for method, status, request payload, response headers, and redirect.
Add a breakpoint in the controller and compare the request data with the bound form object.
Refresh the resulting GET page and explain why the redirect changes the browser history behavior.
practicals.solution: Use the form action with method POST, let Spring Security inject the CSRF token into the Thymeleaf form, bind with @ModelAttribute, and return a redirect after successful mutation.
practicals.output: The browser shows one POST followed by a redirect to a GET page, and the controller receives the submitted values as a typed form object.

quiz.question: Why is the POST-redirect-GET pattern useful after a successful form submission?
options: It prevents every request from being authenticated
It reduces accidental duplicate submissions caused by browser refresh
quiz.answer: It reduces accidental duplicate submissions caused by browser refresh
quiz.explanation: After the POST changes state, redirecting to a GET leaves the refreshed page as a retrieval rather than replaying the original form submission.

summary: HTTP semantics remain visible even when Spring MVC hides low-level servlet plumbing.
Typed form binding and validation provide a clean boundary between untrusted request data and application code.
A redirect after a state-changing POST improves normal browser behavior.

lessons.title: Java Project Structure, Maven, and Dependency Discipline
lessons.description: Turn a set of source files into a predictable build. Focus on Maven coordinates, dependency scopes, configuration separation, and the reason layered boundaries reduce accidental coupling.
learningObjectives: Read a Maven pom as a build contract rather than as a list of arbitrary dependencies.
Separate application configuration from source code and secrets.
Explain why controllers should not own persistence logic and why services are a useful application boundary.

notes.text: A useful package boundary

A small application can use packages for web controllers, application services, persistence repositories, domain entities, DTOs/forms, and configuration. The goal is not ceremony; it is to make ownership and change impact obvious.

items: Keep dependencies minimal and deliberate.
Prefer constructor injection so dependencies are explicit and fields can remain final.
Keep environment-specific values in configuration or environment variables instead of source code.

quiz.question: Which dependency-injection style makes a required dependency explicit at construction time?
options: Reading the dependency from an environment variable
quiz.explanation: The constructor signature records what the class requires and supports straightforward unit testing with explicit collaborators.

summary: Maven describes how the project is built and which external components are required.
Constructor injection keeps application dependencies visible and testable.
Configuration and secrets should not be embedded in Java source code.

lessons.title: Git Workflow and Engineering Communication
lessons.description: Practice the collaborative habits that make internship work reviewable: branch from a known base, make narrow commits, open a pull request, respond to review comments, and document the reason for a change.
learningObjectives: Create a focused branch for one change.
Write commits whose message explains the completed unit of work.
Describe implementation decisions and verification steps in a pull request.

notes.text: A good change is easier to review when its intent is narrow. Keep unrelated formatting churn out of feature commits, and record how you verified behavior.

items: Update local main branch.
Create a topic branch.
Make one coherent change.
Run available checks.
Commit with a concise imperative message.
Push the branch and open a pull request.
Resolve review feedback with additional focused commits or a cleanly amended branch according to team policy.

practicals.title: Prepare a Reviewable Feature Branch
practicals.description: Create a Git workflow for the first internship change and produce a review-ready commit history.
steps: Initialize or clone the project repository.
Create a branch named feature/project-validation.
Add one validation rule and one corresponding test or verification note.
Run the relevant local checks.
Commit with a focused message and inspect the diff before opening a pull request.
practicals.solution:
git switch -c feature/project-validation

git add src/ test/
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Validate project names before persistence"

git push -u origin feature/project-validation
practicals.output: The branch contains only the intended validation change, the staged diff is reviewed before commit, and the commit history clearly communicates the change.

summary: Version control is part of engineering quality, not an afterthought.
Small, reviewable changes reduce debugging and integration cost.
Verification notes make pull requests useful to another engineer.

tasks.title: Design a Maintainable Project Module
tasks.description: Create a small project-management slice with explicit controller, service, repository, and form responsibilities.
tasks.problemStatement: A new web application needs project creation without placing validation, persistence, and HTTP concerns in one class.
objectives: Separate request binding from business logic.
Use constructor injection.
Write a concise README section describing the request flow.
constraints: Do not add a second framework just to solve a layering problem.
tasks.hint: Start at the HTTP boundary with a form object, then move business decisions into a service and persistence into a repository.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service owns the normalization rule while the controller remains concerned with HTTP binding and the repository remains concerned with persistence. The rule is deterministic and easy to unit test.

modules.title: Spring MVC Application Construction
modules.description: Build the web layer using annotated controllers, form binding, validation, view templates, redirects, and error handling.
objectives: Implement controller methods with clear request mappings and response semantics.
Bind and validate typed form objects rather than parsing raw request parameters throughout the application.
Render server-side HTML with Thymeleaf using safe data binding conventions.
Use controller advice and meaningful status handling for expected errors.

lessons.title: Controllers, Routing, and View Models
lessons.description: Create Spring MVC controllers that map URLs to application operations without leaking persistence entities into templates.
learningObjectives: Define route mappings for GET and POST actions.
Use view models/DTOs for presentation data.
Explain the role of DispatcherServlet and handler mappings.

notes.text: Spring MVC resolves a request to a controller method, invokes argument resolvers for things such as form objects and the current principal, and then interprets the return value as either a view name or another HTTP response representation.

practicals.title: Build a Project List and Create Form
practicals.description: Implement a server-rendered project list and creation form using Spring MVC and Thymeleaf.
steps: Create GET /projects and GET /projects/new controller methods.
Create a POST /projects handler accepting a typed ProjectForm.
Return a validation view when binding errors exist.
Redirect to /projects after a successful create.
Render only fields needed by the view model.
practicals.solution: Use separate GET methods for the list and form, a POST method for mutation, and add only view-specific data to the Model. Use Thymeleaf th:field bindings in the template.
practicals.output: Authenticated users can view their project list, open a creation form, submit valid data, and return to the list via redirect.

quiz.question: What is a strong reason to pass a view model to Thymeleaf instead of exposing a JPA entity directly?
options: It decouples presentation fields from persistence structure
It removes the need for validation
quiz.answer: It decouples presentation fields from persistence structure
quiz.explanation: A view model exposes the data required by the template without coupling the UI contract to the persistence model.

summary: Controllers should own HTTP concerns and delegate business rules.
View models are useful boundaries between persistence representation and presentation needs.
GET and POST routes have distinct semantics in normal web application workflows.

lessons.title: Validation and Error Handling
lessons.description: Make invalid input predictable and safe to handle at the web boundary and in the service layer.
learningObjectives: Apply Jakarta Bean Validation annotations to form records/classes.
Explain why controller validation does not replace domain/business validation.
Return user-friendly errors without exposing implementation details.

notes.text: A validation annotation documents an input constraint but cannot by itself establish authorization, uniqueness under concurrency, or other business invariants.

practicals.title: Add Validation and Safe Error Feedback
practicals.description: Add validation to a project form and a controlled error page for an application exception.
steps: Define @NotBlank and @Size constraints on ProjectForm.
Add a BindingResult parameter immediately after the validated argument.
Display field-specific messages in the Thymeleaf view.
Create an exception handler for an expected conflict and return a safe message.
Confirm that unexpected exception details are not rendered to users.
practicals.solution: Use Bean Validation on ProjectForm, inspect BindingResult before invoking the service, and handle known conflicts with @ExceptionHandler or @ControllerAdvice while logging server-side details separately.
practicals.output: Invalid submissions remain on the form with clear validation feedback; known conflicts render a controlled response without stack traces or database details.

quiz.question: What should application code do when a validation failure is caused by a client-submitted project name?
options: Persist it anyway and clean it later
Return controlled validation feedback and avoid persistence
Log the raw password with the error
Expose the SQL exception to the browser
quiz.answer: Return controlled validation feedback and avoid persistence
quiz.explanation: Validation failures are expected input problems and should be handled at the boundary without persisting invalid data or exposing implementation details.

summary: Boundary validation improves error quality but does not replace business rules.
Expected application failures should have deliberate HTTP/user-facing handling.
Sensitive diagnostics belong in server-side logs, not browser responses.

lessons.title: Thymeleaf Forms, Reusable Views, and Accessibility
lessons.description: Build server-rendered pages that remain usable with keyboard navigation, labels, meaningful headings, and robust error presentation.
learningObjectives: Use semantic HTML elements with explicit labels and validation messaging.
Bind Thymeleaf fields without duplicating request parsing code.
Check keyboard and assistive-technology affordances during review.

items: Every form control should have an associated label.
Error messages should identify the affected field and not rely only on color.
Use headings in document order and meaningful button text.

practicals.title: Accessibility Review of a Form
practicals.description: Review a project creation form against basic keyboard, label, focus, and error-message requirements.
steps: Navigate the form using only the keyboard.
Verify the visible label is programmatically associated with the input.
Trigger a validation error and inspect whether the message identifies the field.
Check that the submit action is a native button with descriptive text.
Document one improvement and implement it.
practicals.solution: Add explicit label-for/id pairs, retain native form controls, provide visible error text, and ensure focus order follows the reading order. Use browser accessibility tooling as a supplement to manual keyboard inspection.
practicals.output: The form can be completed without a mouse, labels are associated with inputs, and validation feedback is understandable without relying on color alone.

summary: Semantic HTML and explicit labels make server-rendered forms easier to operate and test.
Accessibility is part of implementation quality, not only a visual polish step.
Thymeleaf can preserve the server-side validation workflow in the rendered page.

lessons.title: Controller Error Boundaries and HTTP Status Codes
lessons.description: Handle not-found, forbidden, and conflict cases deliberately at the web boundary.
learningObjectives: Choose status codes based on the outcome of the request rather than internal exceptions.
Differentiate not-found, forbidden, unauthorized, and conflict semantics.
Keep stack traces and internal persistence details out of client responses.

items: 401 generally concerns missing/invalid authentication at an HTTP security boundary; authenticated users denied access normally receive 403.
404 communicates that the requested resource is not available to the client.
409 is useful when a state conflict prevents an otherwise valid operation, such as a uniqueness conflict.

quiz.question: Which status is appropriate when an authenticated user is denied access to an existing resource?
quiz.explanation: The user is authenticated but lacks permission, so 403 represents the authorization failure.

summary: HTTP status codes are part of the application contract.
Expected errors should map to deliberate user-facing responses.
Internal implementation details should remain server-side.

tasks.title: Implement a Validated Project Creation Flow
tasks.description: Build the project creation slice with typed input, validation, service delegation, controlled conflict handling, and an accessible form.
tasks.problemStatement: Users need a reliable way to create projects while invalid names and duplicate names are handled without exposing database exceptions.
objectives: Create a validated ProjectForm.
Implement controller and service boundaries.
Return a safe conflict response.
Provide field-level validation feedback.
constraints: Do not perform persistence from the Thymeleaf template or controller method body.
tasks.hint: Let the form own input shape, the controller own HTTP flow, and the service own business rules.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The boundary is explicit, invalid input is rejected before persistence, and the redirect follows a successful mutation. The service remains testable without HTML concerns. The service also maps a database uniqueness violation to a controlled conflict, so concurrent requests do not turn an invariant violation into an opaque server error.

modules.title: Persistence with PostgreSQL and Spring Data JPA
modules.description: Design a relational data model, map it to JPA entities, use repositories and transactions, and avoid common persistence-performance mistakes.
objectives: Design tables with primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness constraints, and indexes that support the application model.
Map JPA entities without exposing persistence mechanics directly to the web layer.
Use repositories and transaction boundaries appropriately.
Explain lazy loading, N+1 risks, and why DTOs or projections can make read paths safer.

lessons.title: Relational Modeling for Web Applications
lessons.description: Translate the issue-tracker domain into normalized tables with explicit relationships and constraints.
learningObjectives: Identify one-to-many relationships among users, projects, issues, and comments.
Choose keys and constraints that enforce application invariants at the database boundary.
Add indexes for high-value lookup paths.

notes.text: Database constraints are part of correctness

Application checks improve user experience, but the database remains the final authority for uniqueness and referential integrity. The schema should represent the invariants that must remain true even under concurrent requests.

practicals.title: Inspect a Relational Schema
practicals.description: Use PostgreSQL to create and inspect the core schema constraints and an index used by issue filtering.
steps: Apply the V1 database migration in a PostgreSQL development database.
Inspect table definitions and constraints with psql metadata commands.
Insert a valid project and issue, then attempt an invalid foreign-key insert.
Use EXPLAIN on a query filtering issues by project and status and document whether the designed index is considered.
practicals.solution: Use foreign keys between child and parent tables, a unique constraint on usernames, and an index on the columns used together by common issue filters. Run EXPLAIN rather than assuming the index will always be used.
practicals.output: Valid rows are accepted; invalid foreign-key relationships are rejected by PostgreSQL. EXPLAIN shows the planner's chosen strategy for the actual data distribution.

quiz.question: Why should important uniqueness rules be enforced with a database constraint even when the application checks first?
options: Because two concurrent requests can both pass the application check
Because unique constraints are only needed for reads
quiz.answer: Because two concurrent requests can both pass the application check
quiz.explanation: A pre-check is subject to race conditions. A database uniqueness constraint provides the authoritative protection against duplicate values.

summary: Relational constraints protect invariants under concurrent access.
Indexes should follow real access patterns rather than being added indiscriminately.
EXPLAIN is a measurement tool, not a guarantee about future query performance.

lessons.title: JPA Entities, Repositories, and Query Design
lessons.description: Implement entity mappings and repositories while keeping query intent explicit.
learningObjectives: Map relationships with JPA annotations.
Use Spring Data repository methods for straightforward queries.
Recognize when a repository query needs a projection or explicit join to avoid inefficient access.

notes.text: The compact example above is a mapping fragment, not a project solution. In the capstone file-wise solution, every required class is complete.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a Spring Data repository interface?
options: To provide a consistent abstraction for common persistence operations
To store passwords in source control
quiz.answer: To provide a consistent abstraction for common persistence operations
quiz.explanation: Spring Data repositories reduce boilerplate around persistence operations while allowing application-specific queries when needed.

summary: JPA maps object state to relational persistence, while repositories provide a convenient data-access abstraction.
Query design should consider how data is actually consumed, not only whether a query returns correct rows.
Avoid exposing persistence entities directly when a stable external representation is more appropriate.

lessons.title: Transactions, Concurrency, and Persistence Boundaries
lessons.description: Understand transaction scope and why state-changing operations should have clear transactional boundaries.
learningObjectives: Explain atomicity in a service operation that updates related data.
Use @Transactional at the application-service boundary for multi-step writes.
Recognize race conditions that require database constraints or explicit locking strategies.
summary: Transactions make a unit of work explicit.
Concurrency correctness cannot be delegated to in-memory checks alone; use database constraints and appropriate transaction semantics.
Keep transaction ownership in the application layer that coordinates the related persistence operations.

lessons.title: Read Performance, N+1 Queries, and Pagination
lessons.description: Design list pages that remain predictable as data grows.
learningObjectives: Explain the N+1 query pattern.
Choose pagination for user-facing lists rather than loading unlimited rows.
Use projections or tailored queries when a list needs only a subset of fields.

notes.text: A page displaying 25 issues should not accidentally cause one query for the list plus one query per row for associated data. Measure generated SQL during development and shape read models around the screen's actual needs.

quiz.question: Which technique directly limits the amount of data fetched for a paginated issue list?
options: Loading every issue into a static array
quiz.explanation: Spring Data can apply a Pageable to a repository query so the database returns only the requested page of rows.

summary: Performance problems often come from data-access shape rather than the raw database alone.
Pagination protects user-facing list endpoints from unbounded result sets.
Projection-style reads can avoid loading columns or relationships the page does not need.

tasks.title: Build the Issue Persistence Slice
tasks.description: Implement project, issue, and comment persistence with constraints and a transactional issue-creation path.
tasks.problemStatement: The web application needs durable issue data with ownership references, sensible constraints, and a service operation that creates an issue consistently.
objectives: Create the relational schema.
Map the JPA entities.
Create repository interfaces.
Add a transactional service method.
Add one focused test for issue creation behavior.
constraints: Do not load all issues into memory for a list that can be paginated.
tasks.hint: Start from the relational invariants, then mirror them in entity annotations and use a service transaction for the write workflow.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service validates the project reference before persistence and stores the issue inside a transaction. The database schema still enforces the foreign-key relationship as the final integrity boundary.

modules.title: Forms, Sessions, Authentication, and Authorization
modules.description: Implement secure session-based authentication and server-side authorization using Spring Security, password hashing, CSRF protection, and ownership checks.
objectives: Distinguish authentication from authorization.
Configure session-based form login with a persistent user store.
Use a PasswordEncoder instead of storing plaintext passwords.
Protect state-changing form endpoints from CSRF and enforce authorization at the server boundary.

lessons.title: Authentication Architecture and Password Storage
lessons.description: Build a persistent user authentication path and understand what Spring Security does around the application request.
learningObjectives: Implement UserDetails backed by the application database.
Configure a PasswordEncoder and store only encoded passwords.
Explain the relationship among Authentication, SecurityContext, UserDetailsService, and a session.

notes.text: Never use NoOpPasswordEncoder or store plaintext passwords in an application database.

quiz.question: What should be stored in the user table for a password-based login system?
quiz.explanation: Passwords should be transformed with a suitable password-hashing/encoding strategy. The application verifies a presented password against the stored encoded value rather than recovering plaintext.

summary: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines what that identity may do.
Spring Security can integrate an application-specific UserDetailsService with encoded passwords.
Password storage must use a suitable PasswordEncoder and never plaintext credentials.

lessons.title: Sessions, Form Login, and CSRF Protection
lessons.description: Configure browser sessions and safe form submission in a server-rendered application.
learningObjectives: Describe why session cookies are different from application passwords.
Configure form login and logout paths.
Explain why CSRF protection matters for cookie-authenticated state changes.

notes.text:
http
    .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/css/**", "/login", "/register").permitAll()
        .anyRequest().authenticated())
    .formLogin(form -> form.loginPage("/login").defaultSuccessUrl("/projects", true).permitAll())
    .logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout").permitAll());

items: Keep CSRF protection enabled for browser session flows unless the application's security model explicitly justifies a different design.
Render the CSRF token in every unsafe form submission.
Do not put authentication secrets in query strings.

quiz.question: Why is CSRF protection important for a session-authenticated form?
options: Because the browser automatically sends the session cookie with requests
Because it hashes every HTML element
quiz.answer: Because the browser automatically sends the session cookie with requests
quiz.explanation: A malicious site can attempt to cause a victim's browser to submit a state-changing request while the session cookie is automatically attached. CSRF defenses add a request-specific secret that the attacker cannot normally know.

summary: Cookie-backed sessions create a browser security boundary that must be considered for state-changing requests.
Spring Security supports form login and logout as part of the servlet security chain.
CSRF protection is especially important for browser requests authenticated with cookies.

lessons.title: Authorization, Ownership, and Method Security
lessons.description: Enforce resource ownership and role-based rules on the server rather than trusting UI visibility.
learningObjectives: Implement ownership checks for project and issue resources.
Use roles for administrative capabilities.
Explain why hiding a button is not authorization.

quiz.question: What makes an ownership check an authorization control?
options: It verifies the current user is allowed to act on the requested resource
It hides all buttons in the UI
quiz.answer: It verifies the current user is allowed to act on the requested resource
quiz.explanation: Authorization is a server-side decision about whether the authenticated principal may perform the requested operation on the resource.

summary: Authorization must be enforced on the server for the actual resource being accessed.
Role checks and ownership checks solve different authorization questions and can be combined.
UI visibility can improve usability but cannot replace server-side access control.

lessons.title: Secure Error Handling and Session Hygiene
lessons.description: Prevent information leakage and reduce avoidable session/authentication mistakes.
learningObjectives: Return controlled errors for invalid credentials and forbidden operations.
Avoid logging passwords, session identifiers, or authorization headers.
Explain logout and session lifecycle expectations for a server-rendered application.

items: Authentication failures should not reveal whether a username exists when that information is sensitive.
Application logs should contain enough context to diagnose a failure without recording secrets.
Use TLS in deployed environments so session cookies and credentials are not exposed on the network.
notes.text: Use @EnableMethodSecurity and current authorization mechanisms for new code. Treat older authorization annotations as legacy rather than the default teaching pattern.

quiz.question: Which item should never be written to normal application logs?
options: A password submitted by a user
quiz.answer: A password submitted by a user
quiz.explanation: Passwords are secrets and should never be logged. The same principle applies to session tokens and other credentials.

summary: Error messages should be useful without disclosing sensitive authentication details.
Logs are security-sensitive data stores and must be designed accordingly.
Session security depends on secure transport, cookie controls, and correct logout behavior.

tasks.title: Secure Project and Issue Authorization
tasks.description: Add authentication and ownership-based authorization so users can work only with permitted resources.
tasks.problemStatement: A member can currently reach predictable URLs for projects and issues that they do not own. Prevent insecure direct object reference patterns by checking ownership on every relevant server-side action.
objectives: Implement database-backed login.
Encode passwords.
Add session-based authorization rules.
Protect project and issue read/write operations with ownership checks.
Retain CSRF protection for browser forms.
constraints: Do not rely on disabled buttons or hidden links as an authorization control.
tasks.hint: Create a single authorization boundary in the service layer and call it before loading or mutating protected resources.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service checks the actual persisted owner relationship before a protected operation. UI controls are only presentation; the service remains the final authorization boundary.

modules.title: API Design, JSON DTOs, and Integration
modules.description: Expose a small, deliberate JSON API for issue data while preserving the server-side authorization boundary and stable response contracts.
objectives: Design resource-oriented endpoints with explicit status codes and DTOs.
Validate API input independently from HTML forms.
Protect API resources with the same server-side authorization rules as the web UI.
Test response shapes and failure cases without leaking persistence internals.

lessons.title: REST-Style Resource Design
lessons.description: Design a focused JSON endpoint that exposes issue data without coupling the public representation to the JPA entity.
learningObjectives: Choose a stable resource URL and HTTP method for a read operation.
Return a DTO with only fields required by the API client.
Select status codes for successful and failing resource lookup.

quiz.question: Why is a DTO useful for an API response?
options: It exposes every database column automatically
It lets the API contract be shaped independently of persistence entities
It makes JSON impossible to parse
quiz.answer: It lets the API contract be shaped independently of persistence entities
quiz.explanation: A DTO establishes an explicit external contract and helps keep persistence details out of API responses.

summary: API contracts should be deliberate and smaller than internal persistence models when possible.
HTTP methods and statuses communicate behavior to clients.
Authorization must still be enforced for JSON endpoints.

lessons.title: Request Validation and JSON Error Contracts
lessons.description: Create predictable validation errors for API clients without exposing stack traces or internal exception text.
learningObjectives: Validate JSON request objects with Bean Validation.
Define a consistent error shape for validation failures.
Distinguish client errors from server failures.

quiz.question: What is a good API response for invalid request data?
options: A controlled 4xx response containing safe validation details
A 200 response with a stack trace
A successful redirect to a random page
quiz.answer: A controlled 4xx response containing safe validation details
quiz.explanation: Invalid client input should normally be represented by an appropriate client-error response with information useful to correct the request, without leaking internal diagnostics.

summary: JSON request validation should be explicit and reusable.
Error contracts are part of API design.
Client errors and server errors should not be conflated.

lessons.title: API Authentication and Authorization Boundaries
lessons.description: Integrate API calls with the same security model rather than treating JSON routes as inherently trusted.
learningObjectives: Explain how the authenticated principal reaches an API controller.
Apply ownership checks before returning protected resource data.
Recognize why exposing an identifier in a URL does not grant access.

notes.text: An API route is not secure merely because the browser UI hides it. Any client that can send HTTP requests can attempt to call the route.

summary: API endpoints must enforce authorization independently of presentation-layer controls.
The identity established by Spring Security can be used by controllers and services to enforce access decisions.
Resource identifiers are references, not permissions.

tasks.title: Expose a Secure Issue Read API
tasks.description: Implement an authenticated issue endpoint that returns a stable DTO and denies access to resources outside the current user's project scope.
tasks.problemStatement: A web client needs JSON issue details. The endpoint must return a small response, use appropriate status behavior, and preserve ownership authorization.
objectives: Create an IssueResponse DTO.
Implement the GET endpoint.
Reuse service-layer visibility checks.
Return 404 when the requested resource is unavailable through the caller's permitted scope.
Document a sample request and response shape.
constraints: Do not return the JPA entity directly from the endpoint.
tasks.hint: Apply the same authorization rule used by the HTML page, then map the entity to a dedicated response record.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The API returns only the fields needed by the client. Authorization is performed before mapping, so the API cannot be used to bypass project ownership checks.

modules.title: Testing, Debugging, and Quality Gates
modules.description: Develop confidence through unit tests, MVC/security checks, regression tests, structured debugging, and code-review habits.
objectives: Write focused unit tests for service rules and boundary conditions.
Test controller behavior for validation and authorization outcomes.
Use logs, breakpoints, SQL inspection, and reproducible cases to debug problems.
Review changes for correctness, maintainability, security, and regression risk.

lessons.title: Unit Testing Business Rules
lessons.description: Test deterministic service logic with JUnit and Mockito where collaborators are external to the rule under test.
learningObjectives: Identify the smallest unit that proves a business rule.
Use mocks only for true collaborators and avoid mocking the object under test.
Write a regression test for every bug that is fixed.

quiz.question: What is the best role for a regression test after fixing an authorization bug?
options: Prevent the same security rule from silently breaking again
quiz.answer: Prevent the same security rule from silently breaking again
quiz.explanation: A regression test captures the corrected behavior as an executable expectation.

summary: Unit tests should target clear rules and boundaries.
Security bugs deserve regression tests because later refactors can reintroduce them.
Mocks are tools for isolating collaborators, not substitutes for testing the real behavior everywhere.

lessons.title: MVC and Security Integration Testing
lessons.description: Verify that routing, validation, authentication, authorization, and response handling work together at the web boundary.
learningObjectives: Use Spring's MVC test support to exercise controller behavior.
Include CSRF when testing unsafe browser requests under Spring Security.
Verify both allowed and denied cases rather than only the happy path.

notes.text: A controller unit test can miss security filters, argument resolution, CSRF enforcement, and view rendering. MVC integration-style tests are valuable for proving that those layers still agree about the HTTP contract.

items: Test anonymous access to a protected page.
Test an authenticated member accessing an owned resource.
Test a member attempting another user's resource.
Test an unsafe request with and without the expected CSRF token.

quiz.question: Why should an unsafe form request be tested with CSRF handling when Spring Security protects the application?
options: Because CSRF is part of the security behavior at the HTTP boundary
Because it changes HTML into Java
Because it is required for database indexes
quiz.answer: Because CSRF is part of the security behavior at the HTTP boundary
quiz.explanation: A test that omits the security filter chain can miss the real request behavior. Including CSRF in the test proves the application behaves as deployed through that boundary.

summary: Integration-style web tests prove multiple framework layers interact correctly.
Security behavior should be tested as part of the HTTP contract.
Both positive and negative authorization cases matter.

lessons.title: Debugging a Web Request from Browser to Database
lessons.description: Use evidence instead of guesswork when diagnosing a failed web request.
learningObjectives: Reproduce a failure with stable input.
Use request traces, controller breakpoints, service logs, and SQL inspection to locate the first incorrect boundary.
Change one variable at a time and capture the final root cause.
Create a regression test once the cause is understood.

items: Start from the externally visible symptom and work inward.
Distinguish an input problem from a mapping problem, authorization problem, transaction problem, or database problem.
Do not add retries to hide an unknown root cause.

summary: Reliable debugging is an evidence-gathering process.
The earliest incorrect boundary is often more useful than the final exception line.
A bug is not fully fixed until its corrected behavior is protected by a regression check.

tasks.title: Diagnose and Regression-Test an Authorization Failure
tasks.description: Given a reproducible resource-access defect, trace it across controller and service boundaries, identify the authorization mistake, correct it, and add a regression test.
tasks.problemStatement: An authenticated member can view an issue that belongs to a different project owner. Reproduce the failure, locate the missing authorization check, fix the service boundary, and prove the denial with a test.
objectives: Reproduce the unauthorized access case.
Inspect the request principal and resource owner.
Move the access decision to the service layer if it is only enforced in the UI.
Add a failing test before the fix and a passing regression test after the fix.
Record the root cause in the change documentation.
constraints: Do not fix the issue only by hiding a link in Thymeleaf.
tasks.hint: Follow the resource ID through the controller into the service and verify who owns the referenced project.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The test captures the authorization invariant independently of the UI. The service checks ownership before loading or returning the protected resource, preventing direct URL access from bypassing the rule.

modules.title: Production Readiness: Configuration, Observability, and Deployment
modules.description: Prepare the application for controlled deployment with environment-based configuration, health endpoints, structured operational thinking, containerization, and reproducible startup.
objectives: Separate deploy-time configuration from source code.
Use health checks and safe actuator exposure for operational visibility.
Create a reproducible container build and local multi-container environment.
Document deployment, rollback, logging, and troubleshooting considerations.

lessons.title: Configuration, Secrets, and Environment Separation
lessons.description: Move connection details and deploy-time settings outside the codebase without creating an unsafe configuration story.
learningObjectives: Use environment variables or external configuration for database credentials and application settings.
Keep example configuration non-secret.
Explain the difference between configuration and secrets management in deployment environments.

notes.text: Do not commit real credentials, access tokens, private keys, or production connection strings to source control.

quiz.question: Which value belongs in an environment variable rather than source control?
quiz.explanation: Secrets should be supplied through an appropriate secret/configuration mechanism instead of being committed to source control.

summary: Configuration should vary by environment without requiring source edits.
Real secrets should never be committed to the repository.
Schema validation prevents accidental automatic schema mutation during normal startup.

lessons.title: Health Checks, Actuator, and Operational Signals
lessons.description: Expose only the operational information needed to support deployment and troubleshooting.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between health information and application business endpoints.
Expose the health endpoint intentionally.
Avoid making sensitive operational endpoints public without a clear security model.

notes.text:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true

summary: Health endpoints are operational interfaces and should be treated as security-sensitive surfaces.
Actuator provides standardized operational endpoints; exposure should be deliberate.
Monitoring design should start with the signals needed to detect failure and diagnose it.

lessons.title: Containerization and Local Deployment
lessons.description: Package the application and PostgreSQL dependency into a reproducible local environment using Docker and Compose.
learningObjectives: Build the application in a multi-stage image.
Run the application and PostgreSQL as separate services.
Pass database settings through environment variables.
Use a health check to control startup dependency sequencing where appropriate.

notes.text:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: webapp
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d webapp"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/webapp
      DB_USERNAME: ${POSTGRES_USER}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

quiz.question: Why use a multi-stage Docker build for a Java application?
options: It can keep build tooling out of the final runtime image
It makes passwords safe to commit
It removes the need for tests
quiz.answer: It can keep build tooling out of the final runtime image
quiz.explanation: A builder stage can compile/package the application while the final stage contains only what is needed to run it.

summary: Containers make application/runtime packaging reproducible when configuration is externalized.
Compose can model a local application-plus-database environment.
Health checks help coordinate dependent service startup without embedding arbitrary delays.

lessons.title: Release, Rollback, Logging, and Troubleshooting
lessons.description: Plan operational behavior rather than assuming deployment ends when the container starts.
learningObjectives: Define startup checks and a simple rollback decision.
Keep application logs useful without recording secrets.
Document common failures such as database connectivity and failed migrations.
Describe how to verify a release without inventing test results.

items: A release checklist should include configuration verification, database migration status, health endpoint status, representative smoke tests, and a rollback path.
When troubleshooting database startup, verify DNS/service name, port, credentials, database readiness, and migration errors separately.
A rollback may require both application image rollback and deliberate database compatibility planning.

summary: Deployment is an operational process with verification and rollback, not only an image build.
Logs should support diagnosis without becoming a store of secrets.
Database changes require compatibility thinking because old and new application versions may overlap during rollout.

tasks.title: Containerize the Application Safely
tasks.description: Create a reproducible local deployment that runs the web application with PostgreSQL and supplies all secrets through environment variables.
tasks.problemStatement: The capstone must run locally without hardcoded database passwords. The app should wait for the database to become healthy and expose a safe health endpoint for verification.
objectives: Create a multi-stage Dockerfile.
Create a compose.yml with app and database services.
Use an .env.example file containing only example values.
Configure health checks.
Document build, start, log inspection, smoke-test, and shutdown commands.
constraints: Do not commit a real password into compose.yml or .env.example.
tasks.hint: Keep the image definition declarative and pass deploy-time secrets through the environment. Use a service health check rather than a fixed sleep.
tasks.solutionCode:
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q -DskipTests package

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/web-app.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]
tasks.solutionExplanation: The builder image contains Maven and source; the final image contains the packaged application and a Java runtime. Database credentials are supplied only at deployment time, and the database health check is used for service readiness.

modules.title: Independent Capstone: Secure Issue Tracker
modules.description: Complete the internship by designing, implementing, testing, documenting, and packaging a coherent web application that demonstrates the engineering practices developed across the previous modules.
objectives: Integrate server-rendered web UI, persistent storage, authentication, authorization, API exposure, validation, tests, and containerized deployment.
Make engineering decisions explicit through documentation and a reproducible setup.
Demonstrate secure defaults and explain remaining operational limitations honestly.
Present the finished system as an independently completed engineering artifact.

project.heading: Build a Secure Issue Tracker for Small Engineering Teams
project.description: Build a server-rendered web application that lets authenticated team members create projects, report and manage issues, add comments, and inspect issue data through a small JSON API. The application uses PostgreSQL for durable relational storage, Spring MVC and Thymeleaf for the browser experience, Spring Security for session-based authentication and authorization, Spring Data JPA for persistence, Bean Validation for input constraints, automated tests for business and web behavior, and Docker Compose for reproducible local deployment. The project is intentionally unified rather than split into separate frontend and backend products so the intern learns how a single web application crosses HTTP, presentation, application, persistence, security, and operational boundaries.
project.problemStatement: Small engineering teams need a lightweight place to capture work items without relying on shared spreadsheets or informal messages. The system must preserve ownership boundaries, avoid exposing passwords or database internals, reject invalid input, allow users to view and update only resources they are permitted to access, and provide a small API for machine-readable issue details. The intern is responsible for implementing the application, verifying its behavior, documenting it, and preparing a reproducible local deployment.
objectives: Design a relational schema with users, projects, issues, and comments.
Implement a secure browser login and registration flow.
Implement ownership-aware project and issue operations.
Render accessible HTML forms and list/detail pages with Thymeleaf.
Expose a protected JSON issue endpoint with a stable DTO.
Add validation, controlled error handling, unit tests, and MVC/security tests.
Package the application and PostgreSQL with Docker Compose using environment-supplied credentials.
Document the architecture, setup, security controls, troubleshooting workflow, and release checklist.
requirements: Functional: users can register, sign in, sign out, create projects, view projects they own, create issues in accessible projects, update issue status and priority, add comments, and retrieve an issue through a protected JSON endpoint.
Functional: administrative users can view all projects; normal members are restricted to resources associated with projects they own.

Technical: Java 21 language/runtime compatibility target, Maven build, Spring Boot 4.1.1, Spring MVC, Thymeleaf, Spring Security 7.1.1, Spring Data JPA 4.1.1, PostgreSQL 18, Flyway, JUnit 5, Mockito, Docker, Docker Compose.

Security: encoded password storage, session-based authentication, CSRF protection for browser mutations, server-side authorization, safe error responses, no hardcoded credentials, and no secret logging.
Validation: project names and issue/comment fields must enforce length and blank-value constraints at the request boundary, with business rules rechecked in the service layer.
Quality: focused unit tests for business rules and web/security tests for important authorization and CSRF cases.
Deployment: externalize database connection properties, provide an .env.example file without real secrets, include a health check, and document release verification and rollback considerations.
features: User registration creates a normal MEMBER account; the development environment may seed a known ADMIN account only when an explicit password environment variable is provided.
Project creation validates names, associates each project with its authenticated owner, and rejects duplicates for the same owner.
Issue creation records reporter, project, status, priority, title, and description with server-side authorization.
Issue detail pages show only comments and project data the current user is permitted to view.
Issue update controls allow permitted users to change status and priority while the service revalidates ownership.
Comment creation attributes the author from the authenticated principal rather than trusting a submitted user identifier.
The JSON endpoint returns only a stable IssueResponse DTO and uses the same authorization boundary as the HTML interface.
Operational health is available through a deliberately exposed actuator endpoint rather than exposing all actuator endpoints.

technologyStack.name: Java 21
technologyStack.role: Defines domain, web, persistence, security configuration, and test code
technologyStack.why: Current Java SE documentation provides the language/runtime baseline and long-term support options for modern Java applications.

technologyStack.name: Spring Boot 4.1.1
technologyStack.role: Provides dependency management, auto-configuration, embedded web runtime integration, and production configuration conventions
technologyStack.why: It is the current stable Spring Boot line researched for this internship.

technologyStack.name: Spring MVC
technologyStack.role: Routes HTTP requests, binds input, renders Thymeleaf views, and serves JSON endpoints
technologyStack.why: It provides the conventional request/controller/view programming model used by this application.

technologyStack.name: Spring Security 7.1.1
technologyStack.role: Protects requests, manages sessions, encodes passwords, and supports CSRF protection
technologyStack.why: It provides the required security controls for the browser application.

technologyStack.name: Spring Data JPA 4.1.1
technologyStack.role: Maps entities and repositories to PostgreSQL
technologyStack.why: It reduces persistence boilerplate while preserving explicit repository and transaction boundaries.

technologyStack.name: Thymeleaf
technologyStack.role: Renders accessible forms, lists, validation feedback, and issue detail pages
technologyStack.why: It keeps the internship focused on web application engineering without introducing a second frontend framework.

technologyStack.name: PostgreSQL 18
technologyStack.role: Stores accounts, projects, issues, and comments with constraints and indexes
technologyStack.why: The researched PostgreSQL 18 documentation is the current supported database line used by the project.

technologyStack.name: Flyway
technologyStack.role: Applies versioned SQL schema changes during application startup
technologyStack.why: Versioned migrations make schema evolution explicit and reviewable.

technologyStack.name: JUnit 5 and Mockito
technologyStack.role: Verifies service rules and selected web/security behavior
technologyStack.why: They provide focused tools for unit and integration-style tests.

technologyStack.name: Docker and Docker Compose
technologyStack.role: Packages the application and PostgreSQL as separate services
technologyStack.why: The deployment model mirrors a common local development workflow and keeps credentials externalized.

architecture.style: Layered server-rendered web application with a protected JSON endpoint
layers: Web layer: controllers, forms, DTOs, view models
Application layer: business rules, ownership checks, transactions
Persistence layer: JPA entities and repositories
Operational layer: configuration, health, container deployment
securityBoundaries: Unauthenticated public pages: login, registration, static assets
Authenticated request boundary: Spring Security session authentication and CSRF protection
Authorization boundary: service-level ownership and role checks before protected resource access
Persistence boundary: database constraints and parameterized repository access
architecture.dataFlow: Browser -> HTTP request -> Spring Security filters -> MVC controller -> validation -> application service -> repository -> PostgreSQL -> service result -> controller -> Thymeleaf or JSON response -> Browser

setupInstructions: Install JDK 21 and Maven compatible with the researched Spring Boot system requirements, or use the provided Maven-based container build for the capstone environment.
Create a PostgreSQL 18 development database, or start the provided Compose environment.
Copy .env.example to .env for local Compose use and replace example values locally; never commit real secrets.
Run `mvn test` to execute the automated test suite when Maven is installed.
Run `mvn spring-boot:run` for a local host-based development run, or run `docker compose up --build` for the containerized setup.
Open the application at port 8080, register a normal member account, and create a project before exercising issue features.
For a development administrator, set `APP_SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` in the environment before starting the application. The application should never derive an admin account from a hardcoded password.
implementationSteps: 1. Create the Maven project and verify the Java/Spring Boot baseline.
2. Add web, Thymeleaf, validation, JPA, PostgreSQL, Flyway, Security, and Actuator dependencies.
3. Create the migration with users, projects, issues, comments, constraints, and indexes.
5. Implement registration with validation and password encoding.
6. Configure form login, logout, CSRF protection, and static-resource access.
7. Implement ownership-aware project and issue services.
8. Implement accessible Thymeleaf pages for projects, issues, and comments.
9. Add the JSON issue DTO and protected API endpoint.
10. Add unit tests for authorization and issue rules.
11. Add MVC/security tests for protected routes, validation, and CSRF behavior.
12. Configure Flyway validation, environment-based database settings, and safe actuator exposure.
13. Build the multi-stage Docker image and Compose environment.
14. Perform manual smoke tests and capture the observed results in the intern's own work log rather than inventing results.
15. Complete a security review against the OWASP and Spring Security guidance referenced in this internship.
16. Complete README setup, architecture, troubleshooting, and release documentation.
17. Review the final diff for secrets, debug endpoints, accidental broad authorization, and dead code.
18. Package and present the completed application as the final internship assessment.

strategy: Service unit tests for ownership, validation, and state transitions
MVC/security tests for authentication, authorization, and CSRF-sensitive mutations
Manual smoke tests for the main browser flows
Database migration validation during application startup
requiredChecks: Anonymous users cannot open protected project pages.
A member cannot read or modify another owner's project or issue.
Invalid form input returns controlled validation feedback.
Unsafe browser mutations require CSRF protection.
Password values never appear in normal logs or source files.
The API does not return persistence-only fields.

controls: Database foreign keys and unique constraints
threats: Insecure direct object reference through predictable resource IDs
Credential leakage through source or logs
Over-posting or trusting submitted user identifiers
Information leakage through raw exception responses
verificationApproach: Attempt unauthorized URLs as a member account.
Submit mutations without a valid CSRF token and verify the request is rejected.
Inspect repository and configuration files for credentials.
Review comments and issue creation to ensure author identity comes from Authentication rather than form input.

focus: Paginate or constrain issue lists rather than loading unbounded data
Add indexes that match high-value lookup patterns
Avoid N+1 access when rendering issue lists
Use DTOs/projections for narrow API reads
Measure database queries with PostgreSQL EXPLAIN when performance is in doubt
measurementPlan: Capture SQL generated during representative list and detail requests.
Run EXPLAIN on the most important filtered queries.
Measure page response time under a representative local dataset.
Record observations and environment details rather than claiming an unsupported benchmark.

deployment.architecture: Docker Compose local deployment with separate application and PostgreSQL services
releaseChecklist: Build the application image from the reviewed commit.
Verify environment variables are set through the deployment mechanism.
Confirm database health before application verification.
Run representative authenticated and unauthorized smoke tests.
Review logs for errors without exposing secrets.
deployment.rollback: Keep the previous application image available and ensure database migrations are compatible with the rollback strategy. Database migrations are not automatically reversible merely because an application image can be rolled back.

troubleshooting: If the application cannot connect to PostgreSQL, verify the hostname matches the Compose service name, the port is correct, credentials are present, and the database health check is passing.
If a form receives a CSRF failure, inspect whether the rendered form contains the current token and whether the request is submitted through the expected session.
If a member receives 403 unexpectedly, inspect the persisted owner relationship and the service-layer authorization rule rather than changing the UI.
If migrations fail, inspect the Flyway error first and compare the schema version with the application entity expectations.
If a list page becomes slow, inspect generated SQL and query cardinality before adding arbitrary caching.
If Maven cannot compile the project, verify that the JDK in the active shell matches the Java version configured in pom.xml and that Maven resolves the Spring Boot parent and dependencies.
If a template fails because a model attribute is missing, trace the controller branch that returns the view and ensure every field used by Thymeleaf was added before the return.
If an authenticated member can reach an unauthorized route, reproduce the URL directly and trace the service authorization path before changing any template condition.

fileWiseSolution.explanation: Runs the application and database as separate services, uses environment-supplied credentials, and makes the app wait for a healthy database.
fileWiseSolution.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: webapp
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d webapp"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/webapp
      DB_USERNAME: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      APP_SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${APP_SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

fileWiseSolution.explanation: Provides the minimum information another engineer needs to understand, run, verify, troubleshoot, and review the capstone.
fileWiseSolution.code:
# Secure Issue Tracker

## Requirements

- JDK 21 for the primary development target.
- Maven compatible with the Spring Boot 4.1.1 system requirements.
- PostgreSQL 18 for a host-based database run, or Docker and Docker Compose for the containerized run.

## Local configuration

For Compose, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and replace the example values locally. Never commit real secrets.

For a host-based run, export:

```text
DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/webapp
DB_USERNAME=webapp
DB_PASSWORD=<local-secret>
APP_SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<optional-local-admin-password>
```

## Run with Maven

```bash
mvn test
mvn spring-boot:run
```

## Run with Docker Compose

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

The application listens on port 8080. Register a member account, sign in, create a project, and create an issue before testing the protected routes.

## Security notes

- Passwords are stored only in encoded form.
- Browser mutations use Spring Security CSRF protection.
- Resource authorization is enforced server-side with project ownership checks.
- Database credentials come from configuration, not source code.
- Normal logging must never contain passwords, session identifiers, or bearer tokens.

## Troubleshooting

- Database connection failures: verify the service name, credentials, and PostgreSQL health state.
- Flyway failures: inspect the migration error before changing `ddl-auto`; the application uses schema validation.
- 403 responses: verify the authenticated account and persisted project owner before changing the UI.
- CSRF errors: inspect the rendered form for the current CSRF token and verify that the request is a browser session request.

howItWorks.startupFlow: Spring Boot starts, validates the PostgreSQL schema through Flyway/JPA, registers the Spring Security filter chain, and optionally seeds the development admin account only when APP_SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD is explicitly supplied.
howItWorks.authenticationFlow: A registration POST passes a validated username and raw password to AuthService, which normalizes the username and stores an encoded password. On login, Spring Security calls CustomUserDetailsService and compares the presented password with the stored encoded value.
howItWorks.authorizationFlow: The authenticated principal is attached to the request. Controllers pass the principal to services. ProjectService and IssueService verify ownership or ADMIN role before protected reads or writes. The same rule is used by HTML and JSON paths.
howItWorks.requestFlow: Browser request -> SecurityFilterChain -> Controller -> Bean Validation -> Service authorization and business rule -> Repository -> PostgreSQL -> Controller -> Thymeleaf HTML or DTO-based JSON response.
howItWorks.commentFlow: The authenticated principal identifies the author. The service loads the containing issue and checks project visibility before persisting the comment, so a caller cannot impersonate another author through a form field.
howItWorks.deploymentFlow: Docker Compose starts PostgreSQL with a health check, then builds and starts the application. Runtime database configuration is supplied through environment variables; the application health endpoint is used for operational verification.

project.finalProjectExplanation: The capstone demonstrates an end-to-end server-side web application boundary. HTTP requests enter Spring Security before reaching controllers; validation constrains request data; service classes own business rules and authorization; repositories persist normalized relational state; Thymeleaf renders accessible pages; the JSON endpoint uses a DTO rather than an entity; tests capture critical authorization and web-boundary behavior; configuration and container files make the local deployment reproducible. The architecture intentionally keeps authorization in the service layer so it is shared by the browser and API interfaces. The database schema enforces foreign keys, uniqueness, and query-supporting indexes. The result is a realistic internship artifact that can be extended with additional workflows without changing its security boundary.

modules.assessment: Final project is assessed by functional completeness, authorization correctness, validation quality, tests, code organization, documentation, reproducible setup, and the intern's ability to explain design decisions and debug a demonstrated failure. No employment or accreditation outcome is implied.

evaluation.approach: Evaluation is evidence-based: the intern submits module deliverables, explains selected design decisions, demonstrates tests, and completes the capstone review.
evaluation.finalEvaluation: The final review checks whether the intern can explain the request flow, implement or modify a feature without bypassing the architecture, diagnose a failing behavior, write a regression test, identify a security weakness, and operate the finished application from documented setup instructions.
evidenceRequired: Automated test execution output produced by the intern

workflow: Requirement clarification -> small design -> implementation -> automated verification -> review -> fixes -> documentation -> integration -> release verification
Use browser developer tools and application/database logs as evidence when debugging.
Keep authorization and validation rules close to the application boundary that can enforce them consistently.
currentPracticeNotes: Spring MVC is the servlet-stack web framework used here; the internship does not add WebFlux because the capstone is intentionally server-rendered.
Spring Security method security is taught with @EnableMethodSecurity and modern authorization expressions; legacy authorization annotations should not be introduced as the primary design.
Spring Data JPA repositories are used for routine persistence access, while query shape and transactions are reviewed explicitly.

Java uses the JDK 21 LTS baseline for reproducible local compilation in the internship environment. Java SE also publishes newer releases, but the capstone does not require a latest-release migration exercise.
